brief: Something to keep my sewing supplies tidy.

requirements.requirement: Keep sewing supplies tidy (separate storage for small and large items)
requirements.evidence: There are 3 bins on 3 bases: a 3-compartment bin at (0,0), a 2-compartment bin at (1,0) and an undivided full-depth bin at (0,1). That gives 6 separate spaces for different supplies.

The bases are joined by 3 joint bolts (lockJoints), and the outside faces are closed with 12 solid end caps (capOpenFaces). check_build passes and the collision check reads clear. This covers fit only; I can't say anything about strength.
The catalog has no sewing props, so stand-ins are placed: a tape measure, a marker, a pen, a paint brush and a roll of electrical tape for a thread spool.

finish.summary:
I built an open, three-cell sewing caddy. Three hex bases sit in a triangle, joined by 3 joint bolts, with the outside faces closed by 12 solid end caps. Each cell has a different drop-in bin so you can sort by size:
- **3-compartment bin:** for small things like pins, needles and buttons.
- **2-compartment bin:** for thread spools, bobbins and marking pens or chalk.
- **Undivided full-depth bin:** for scissors, tape measures and bigger items.

The configurator's checks pass and its collision check reads clear. There are 18 parts in all, an estimated 1,600 g of filament and about 37 hours of printing.

The catalog has no sewing props, so I staged it with stand-ins:
- a tape measure standing upright in the undivided bin
- a marker and a pen standing in the 3-compartment bin
- a paint brush and a roll of electrical tape in the 2-compartment bin

The roll of tape (standing in for a spool of thread) sits below the bin rim, so you can see it from above but not from the side. Three stand-ins wouldn't place: a pencil and a ruler in those compartments, and tweezers in the 3-compartment bin, so I left them out. The design is open trays with no lid.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
